utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ilic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The cross-examination by Mr. Hannis will continue in a moment. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you gave at the beginning of your evidence continues to apply throughout your evidence. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ilic. The first thing I want to ask you about is the document that is our Exhibit Number P3121. With the usher's help, I'll hand you a hard copy. This is the minutes of a meeting held on 28 July 1998 at the MUP staff in Pristina. I know you didn't attend this meeting, but I've got a couple of questions for you about some things that were discussed there. On the first page of the hard copy you have, and I think it's page 3 in the e-court in B/C/S and in English, General Lukic is speaking, he welcomes the minister, and about five sentences up in that first paragraph under his name, he mentions that: "The second phase of the global plan is being carried out in accordance with the established schedule with ten detachments." In Kosovo, in July of 1998, or any time during your deployment there in 1998, did you hear a discussion of such a plan, the global plan or the five-phase plan for combatting terrorism, anything like that? Did you ever hear that term discussed?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of that term during my preparation for this testimony. I didn't hear of it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If you'll go to the second paragraph then, I think it's the last few lines on the bottom of that page for you, General Lukic apparently says: "In some police units, Nis, Leskovac, Pirot, Kosovska Mitrovica, and Belgrade, there was some lack of readiness and 'reluctance' to be deployed and even refusal to carry out tasks, but this situation has now been resolved." Do you know what that's a reference to? Did you see anything like that or experience anything like that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what this actually refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And if you could turn over the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the English, we can stay on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the bottom of that paragraph, General Lukic says: "We need at least 2.000 additional policemen, especially, if possible, volunteers from the police reserve force." And immediately following him, going onto the next page in English, Minister Stojiljkovic says: "That's a change to the main plan." General Lukic says: "Yes." Were you aware of this call for additional volunteers at the end of July 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to the question as it misstates the document. If he's going to ask a question relating to a document that this witness was not present for, he needs to stick exactly to what is in the document. The document says volunteers from the reserve portion of the police. It doesn't say anything about additional volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question was adequately formulated on the basis of the narrative Mr. Hannis gave, so you can answer that question, Mr. Ilic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In July and August, we did have police reservists among our forces engaged in Kosovo as a part of our detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And does this relate to the problem you mentioned yesterday about policemen being brought in to serve in the PJP who had not undergone the special training or selection process?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a different issue relating to 1999 and the close of our engagement in Kosovo. It was towards the end of our presence in Kosovo, and referring to the active police force. This text, however, refers to the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. If you could continue onto I think it's page number 6 in the hard copy you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is probably page number 8 in e-court for the B/C/S, it's page number 7 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you about something that Captain Pesic is described as having spoken about. Do you find the reference to him?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And he said: "We formed 240 reserve police stations." He mentions weapons have been issued to 54.683 persons, and he describes how those were distributed between from the MUP and from the VJ. Did you have any dealings at all with reserve police during your time in Kosovo in either 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the detachment, we did have a reserve police force from Belgrade; it was in July and August, I believe. As regards reserve police departments in Kosovo, we had no contact with them. I didn't even know they existed. When being proofed for the testimony, they explained to me what the term actually stands for.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If you would look at the bottom of that page and the top of the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for us following in English, we need to go to page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you about something General Lukic says. He's quoted as saying: "We are also arming citizens in towns, and plans for defending towns have been drawn up. Chiefs of secretariats have the duty to organize the defence of towns in agreement with the Yugoslav Army, reserve police stations, and other bodies." Did you, you or your PJP unit, have any role or any knowledge of the citizens in towns being armed and plans for defending towns drawn up? Did you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. During the war, I wasn't in Pec itself. It strikes me as illogical. Had there been such a plan, I should have been in town defending the town; therefore, I had nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you a couple questions from one other document that you probably never saw before coming here, but it relates to some of the things you told us about. You recall, yesterday, I showed you a photograph and you recognised Mr. Radosavljevic and some other people, including someone you thought might be Salipur and who other people indicated was Salipur. Did you ever -- do you recall hearing the term "Munja" used in connection with Salipur?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that. It was a call-sign of one of the companies from the 124th Intervention Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I want to ask you about something that's in a -- in these notes from meetings of the Joint Command in 1998, and I think you told us yesterday you didn't know anything about the Joint Command in 1998 or 1999; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will tell you that, at page 31 of the English and page 23 of the B/C/S in Exhibit P1468, these are the notes of a meeting on the 30th of July, 1998. General Djordjevic is apparently at the meeting and speaks, and he mentions that: "The Munja lunch will be held in the vicinity of Ovcarevo." Do you know anything about that event on 30 July 1998?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has already said he knows nothing about any Joint Command. There's been no foundation as for whether -- if Mr. Hannis is claiming that the witness was present for this meeting, I have yet to hear any foundation for it. Therefore, I believe that the question is just requesting out of thin air to ask for speculation about something that is in some document of questionable -- of questionable source to have him comment on something that's in a document. That's pure speculation after the witness has said already in direct and it in cross that he knows nothing about the existence of this body, and there is no foundation that he was present for this event or this meeting or whatever you want to call it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness has already indicated that he recognises the name Munja. The question's perfectly appropriate. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Ilic, do I need to repeat my question or do you recall it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the text on the screen. You are asking me whether I know something about a lunch at Ovcarevo with Munjas. I don't know anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, one other thing I want to ask you about from these notes, Joint Command meetings - it is from page 77 in the English, and it's page 69 in e-court for the B/C/S - is from a meeting of the 27th of August, 1998. General Lukic is speaking, and he said: "This morning about 320 MUP members and Combat Group 22 began moving towards Klecka, encountering no resistance along the way." Do you know who Combat Group 22 was?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And further down, under the same entry, General Lukic mentions Stimlje-Dulje, and he says: "250 men from MUP pick up note." And I think you told us yesterday that, on the 28th of August, you were in the Dulje area, I think maybe specifically near Blace village. Do you know what that's a reference to, "Stimlje-Dulje, 250 men from MUP pick up note"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I suspect this is one we ought to get the witness to read? Mr. Ilic, the reference to Stimlje-Dulje in the document in front of you, could you read aloud that line, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That page in B/C/S is not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It should be page 68 in the B/C/S; page 77 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. That looks more like it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I misspoke earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: About halfway down the page, Mr. Ilic, you'll see the line with "Stimlje" as the first word. Could you read that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Stimlje-Dulje - 250 men MUP," and I cannot read the two last words.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How many men were in the group that you were deployed with on the 28th of August?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 70 and 80 policemen from my company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, can you assist at all in what these words are?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could be as translated; it resembles that. It's difficult to interpret another person's handwriting. It could be what it stands in the translation. Well, it could also mean "took over elevations."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm finished with that. I'll now move to my notes regarding your answers to some questions yesterday. At page 34 of the transcript, you mentioned -- I think this was in connection with the document, the order signed by Colonel Kotur. And in an answer to a question about that, you mentioned there were problems within the chain of command, "namely, between my commander, Bosko Buha, and Colonel Kotur. Buha told me about that. Because of that issue a few days later, after Bosko Buha had been wounded, General Obrad Stevanovic arrived to deal with it." Now, what kinds of problems was Buha having in the chain of command with Colonel Kotur? Can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Colonel Kotur had wrong information on our positions. The information he had was that we failed to reach the position designated in an order; however, we did, and the issue was resolved during an extremely brief meeting. After two minutes the situation was clear when I explained at what positions we actually were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that the only problem you were aware of that led to Stevanovic coming to deal with?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the only problem that I knew of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that there was a meeting with General Stevanovic to deal with that problem, and you said you attended the meeting as Buha's deputy because he had been wounded a couple of days before. You said, in addition to Stevanovic, there were other attendees, including commanders of police stations participating in the action, as well as commanders of the SAJ, commander of the 23rd Detachment, Josipovic, and several army colonels. Before this meeting, did you know who Kotur was? You had met him, right, and you recognised him? You would know him if you saw him, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. But before I answer, it was interpreted that you said that commanders of police stations who participated in the action were in attendance, which is incorrect. Police detachment commanders who were part of the action attended, as well as SAJ commanders; and on the part of the army, all of those officers present were colonels, I believe. I knew Colonel Kotur from the Klecka action. I could recognise him; although, I cannot recall whether he was in attendance. In any case, I recall that we had no conversation on -- at that meeting. That is precisely why I cannot recall whether he was there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have a few more questions about that meeting. How did this meeting get set up? I mean, when was it held approximately?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, which question is Mr. Hannis staying with because if it's the first one -- if the first one is part of his question, I'm going to object because it calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, right now, I'm just asking when was it held, approximately?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately one or two days after Bosko Buha was wounded. I think he was wounded in early June, on the 1st or the 2nd of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did you come to attend this meeting? Who invited you or told you to come?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the commander of the 23rd Detachment, Borisa Josipovic, that I received further orders from after Bosko Buha had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall where the meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhere in the area of Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who led the meeting? Who seemed to be in charge?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe General Obrad Stevanovic held the highest rank; although, I cannot remember whether he led the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you told us before you don't recall if Kotur was there, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But Kotur must have been talked about in this meeting, right, because wasn't the problem in the chain of command related directly to him?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I recall, the problem was not directly in relation to Colonel Kotur. He led the action very well. We had no special issues with him. The problem was misinformation. I don't know how, but Colonel Kotur had wrong information on our positions. One of the army officers at the meeting - I cannot recall who since I didn't know those army officers - said that our detachment failed to carry out the task as ordered since we were still at our initial positions five or six days into the action. I responded by saying that that is incorrect. And by using the map where the map decision was, that is, the decision on the task, I indicated what our precise position was. So the misunderstanding was resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall if General Lukic attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. He did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 38 yesterday, you were asked about whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move to that, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In dealing with this yesterday, Mr. Ilic, you said that: "There were problems within the chain of command, namely, between my commander, Bosko Buha, and Colonel Kotur. My commander, Buha, told me about that." Now, that sounds like something else, different from the issue you've just dealt with. What were these problems within the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem was in the chain of informing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, what was the nature of the problem that Bosko Buha told you about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the problem. I don't know how they resolved that misunderstanding of theirs. I dealt with it by way of a single sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not following this, I'm afraid. You were told about a problem - about problems - not a problem, but problems, within the chain of command between these two. You were told by Buha. Now, that sounds like something different from the misinformation issue, which you were able to deal with in a moment, you say. So what were the problems between Buha and Colonel Kotur? Please tell us what these are. We are here to find out the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am telling you the truth. There was a problem between Colonel Kotur and Commander Bosko that was created due to the poor information Colonel Kotur had. I don't know how it came about that Colonel Kotur was misinformed. I don't know exactly how intensive the misunderstanding between the two was, whether there was an argument or not. However, that was explained to me as being the basic problem, and I believe that was one of the main reasons for the meeting at which General Obrad Stevanovic was present. When I arrived at the meeting, I saw that, indeed, it was the basic problem that existed between Colonel Kotur and Commander Bosko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, you had dealt with that issue, so what was it that Stevanovic was there for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He probably had a task in his own assessment. He believed he needed to be present at the meeting. He didn't know exactly what the problem was in the chain of command. I don't know exactly, but I can presume that it was his assumption that the problem was greater.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. You were at this meeting. So what was the issue that Stevanovic was there to deal with, and how did he deal with it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to repeat this very clearly. Army officers were at that meeting and officer, or rather, commanders of the PJP; and, among them, I was there too as Bosko Buha's deputy. The army officers said at that meeting then that I, or rather, that my detachment had not carried out our task in accordance with the order initially given because we were still at our initial positions. I said that that was not correct, and I said that we were at different positions. That was all, as far as our problems are concerned with the army, or rather, Colonel Kotur. I think that it wasn't actually a problem; it was a misunderstanding, rather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the meeting lasted two minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The meeting lasted longer than that; however, the problem was resolved within two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what was the rest of the meeting about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After that, I think that Obrad Stevanovic spoke. I can't remember exactly, but it had to do with the further course of the action, the tasks during the course of the action, nothing special. I can't remember any details. There was nothing in particular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'll ask you again, Mr. Ilic. What was the rest of the meeting about? This is a very senior person in the MUP attending a meeting with other senior people, including army officers that you're present at, a meeting at which you have to deal with a particular problem which is resolved. The meeting continues after that with your most senior man present. Please tell us what the rest of the meeting was about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot remember exactly what it was that we talked about. I can just give you a general answer, that the meeting as it continued pertained to, or rather, was geared towards moral and psychological preparation of a kind. In terms of this action having to be completed in accordance with the order, it had to be done completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So nobody discussed how we might have better communications between the army and the MUP as a result of the issue which you had been able to deal with? That was never discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I think that that was not discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Ilic, yesterday, at page 38, you were asked a series of questions by Mr. Ivetic about whether you undertook any action based on a written order or a map decision that had been entitled "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija," or signed by the MUP staff in Pristina, or on the order of any chief of the secretariat of the interior. Your answer to each of those three questions was no. But you don't know, or in 1998 and 1999, you didn't know how anyone higher in the chain of command other than either your immediate superior one level up - and I think you told us on one occasion Buha told you about an order that came from Kotur - but other than that, you didn't know who was higher up in the chain that might have been generating the orders that eventually came down to you; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, besides that one time when you -- when Buha told you about Kotur being the one, were there any other times or parts where you did know more about higher up the chain from where an order came?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't mind this question at all; but when ends, it says "to who?" You know, he asked him about Bosko Buha, and do you know from what level this order came, but to who? It is too general for us to draw a conclusion. The witness is talking about his own chain of command, if I understand Mr. Hannis correctly, and he says that Bosko Buha issued orders to him. Now, the Prosecutor is asking who gave orders to Bosko Buha. Is that the question, or is he asking something else? I really do not understand this; it's not clear to me. If he's asking who gave orders to Bosko Buha, that's the way he should phrase the question. This way, it's in very general terms; it's very broad. I really don't know what kind of conclusions you can draw on the basis of this. I beg your pardon, I really waited to hear all the answers before waiting to say this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question's been answered, Mr. Fila. So we'll move onto something else, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were also asked by Mr. Ivetic, at page 40 yesterday: "Did you during the course of the war in 1999 hear or otherwise find out about massacres of Albanian civilians on the part of the police, specifically in places such as Meja, Izbica, Djakovica, Mala Krusa, Bela Crkva, Suva Reka, or Kotlina." Then you said: "Excuse me. Did you ask me during the war?" The question was: "Yes." Your answer was: "No." Did you have occasion after the war to hear anything about massacres of Albanian civilians on the part of the police in any of those locations I named?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said was that during the course of the war, I had not heard of these massacres; however, the massacre in Podujevo is not mentioned here, the one that I found out about a few days after it took place. We know who the perpetrators were, and we knew what was done about that. So as regards these massacres, I found out about them after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did you find out about them after the war?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Meja, I think it was in 2002 or 2003 through the media; Izbica, sometime in 2001, likewise; as for Djakovica, to this day, I don't know of that massacre. Does that refer to Meja or Djakovica in particular? I don't know that; Mala Krusa, this is the first time I hear of it; Bela Crkva, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about Suva Reka or Kotlina?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Suva Reka, around 2001 or 2002; and Kotlina, this is the first time I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Suva Reka, in 2001 or 2002, did you hear about that through the media or some other source?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, through the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you hear about Colonel Mitrovic being alleged to have been involved in that incident in Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about that when he was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Finally, we have an exhibit, P1723, which is a report from General Lazarevic in May of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let's see if I can hand you a copy of that. Were you aware of the existence of any mixed MUP and VJ check-points in 1999 in Kosovo during the war?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the existence of these check-points. They stopped me a few times, too, and they conducted checks, although I was wearing a uniform and although I was in an official vehicle. As far as I can remember, I was moving along the axis towards Podujevo; that's where I was stopped. The army check-point was an independent one, a self-contained one, so it was only the army at that check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I want to ask you a question about something General Lazarevic says here, and it's the fifth bullet point down from the overall paragraph at the beginning. He says: "The work of mixed check-points of the MUP and the military police units is fraught with problems ..." --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. With your permission, I think that this witness cannot give relevant information in relation to a document that was issued by a completely different structure and at a completely different level. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's hear what the question is and see if he can deal with it. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It says: "The work of these mixed check-points ... is fraught with problems and salient issues since the MUP tolerates criminal activities of its members against the Siptar civilian population - murder, rape, looting, robbery, aggravated theft ..." Did you experience any of that? Did you see MUP tolerating crimes by its members against the Siptar civilian population?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I know it's a pointless objection, Your Honour, but this was asked yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well don't make it --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It was asked and answered yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. If someone answers a question in chief -- are you saying in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, this doesn't stop your opponent cross-examining on it. Mr. Hannis, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do I need to repeat the question, Mr. Ilic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no need for that. I don't know of the Ministry of the Interior or any unit tolerating the commission of such crimes. As for my own unit, I can say quite precisely that we prosecuted such cases. What is stated here is the theft of motor vehicles in particular. We have an officer who was charged with regard to that kind of crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And remind me, again, how many men were in the unit that you commanded in 1999, approximately?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not under my command; they were under the command of Bosko Buha therefore. There were about 400 of them; however, this number went down as the war was nearing its end due to the losses sustained by the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, apart from being an assistant, weren't you a company commander for part of that time?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was a company commander, and I was assistant commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as a company commander, you had approximately 120 men under you, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was up to 80 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ilic, before you first went to Kosovo, you knew the position then held by Mr. Lukic within the SUP in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was that position?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assistant chief of the secretariat of the interior in Belgrade for police affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you on occasion meet him in the course of your work?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How frequently?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1993 until 1996, I was commander of a police station in Belgrade. Then, roughly once a month, we had meetings in the secretariat in Belgrade; and, at these meetings, General Lukic was present, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And then after 1996, between then and 1998, did you meet him from time to time?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the job I had then. It wasn't indispensable for me from that position to attend these meetings; so, therefore, we did not meet up. Sometimes perhaps in the corridors, but that is insignificant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How did you learn that he was being moved to a post in Kosovo ?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I found out from my own superior officer in my home unit in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did he tell you officially?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't think so, but I cannot remember exactly now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have I understood correctly that Mr. Lukic was the assistant head of the department of which you were part within the Belgrade SUP?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was assistant chief of the secretariat in Belgrade, while the unit where I worked, that is to say, the police administration, was only an organizational entity of that secretariat; that is to say, that that is much lower than the position he had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but you described him as the assistant chief of the secretariat of the interior in Belgrade for police affairs. All I'm asking you is whether I've understood rightly that he is somewhere towards the top of the pyramid of the department that you are part of much further down?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly, exactly. Your understanding is correct. He was the number two man in the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So are you saying there was no official announcement to the staff of the secretariat that he was being moved to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such thing, whether there was an official announcement, but I can assume there was at one of these meetings that were held at the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What did you understand was the role he was to play in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't give it any thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. My question was: What did you understand, from being told by your own boss that he was moving, what did you understand was the role he was to play?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't say, I mean my commanding officer, that he was transferred. He said that he was sent to Kosovo, but he didn't say anything more than that to me in any greater detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you say to us that you had no interest in what he would be doing in Kosovo, even when you were sent there yourself?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, I had a lot of other work and a lot of other interests. Perhaps I was interested; but on the basis of that interest, I could not form an opinion or a judgement as to what it was that he was doing there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So, for all you knew, he was being put in charge of all police affairs in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the very logic of things, that is what one could infer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I take it from that answer that he was senior enough in the police to be posted at that point to be in charge of all police affairs in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what one could conclude, but I don't know whether that would be the correct conclusion to draw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate that. Re-examination, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll start with the questions from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Obrad Stevanovic in your testimony yesterday and today. Do you have knowledge if Mr. Obrad Stevanovic was senior to Mr. Lukic within the structure of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know how frequently Mr. Stevanovic was present in Kosovo during 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. The previous question, does it pertain to 1998 and 1999 or does it pertain to the period before 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's do two questions: During 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During 1998 and 1999, I don't know; but if you're asking me about the period before 1998, then that is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if it sets your mind at ease, I'm not suggesting for a moment that Mr. Stevanovic was not senior to Mr. Lukic. My questions were of an entirely different nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand that, and my questions are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And, indeed, the answer to the question who is more senior in the structure won't be gleaned from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: From this witness, correct, correct. That's why I asked the other question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know, during 1999, during the Kosovo war, how frequently Mr. Obrad -- General Obrad Stevanovic was present on the terrain -- was present in Kosovo and Metohija, if you know?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him two or three times, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how about General Djordjevic, do you know if he was -- strike that. Let's move onto my other questions. Today, you talked about reservists that were in your formation in 1998, police reservists. What -- were these police reservists engaged in regular duties in your Belgrade SUP before being sent to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These were citizens who were doing their own jobs. They were civilians, that is to say, working in their own companies, different organizations, and they were engaged in Kosovo as police reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were they within the formation structure of the SUP Belgrade under the plan for the active and reserve police within the SUP Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sometime in 1992/1993, around those years, successively.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No further re-examination for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one other matter, Mr. Ilic. When you returned to Belgrade from Kosovo, which we understand was on a number of occasions, between June 1998 and June 1999 effectively, what position did you then hold in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, I was working with a police brigade. Don't be confused by the name. Just because of the 122nd Intervention Brigade, I was working with the police brigade and I was assistant commander there. That was my original unit; it was the unit I belonged to at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Between your shifts or stints in Kosovo, when you were in Belgrade, were you resting simply or were you active in your position as assistant commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was active, except on long weekends, and those would sometimes last for as long as five or six days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what was the nature of the work done by that brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The focus of our work was on securing public gatherings, especially football matches that were deemed to be of high risk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that brigade, therefore, also a PJP unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is part of the 122nd Intervention Brigade, part of that police brigade is. There is another part that isn't: The Konjic [as interpreted] unit, dog handlers, and units securing the headquarters of the police brigade itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just for the clarity, 24, line 25, "Konjic unit," it is not. It is the "unit of horses" actually, it's not the "Konjic unit."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, dog handling and horses?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, that's right, which is -- but Konjic is a city in Bosnia, that's why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. I've now forgotten my next question, Mr. Zecevic. Just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean that from 1997, or perhaps 1996, until the end of the war your whole working time was engaged in the PJP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was with the PJP from the time it was first set up in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But our understanding is that police officers or a policeman may do a routine job in the SUP where they work and be only part of the time part of the formation of the PJP. Is that a correct understanding of the position of most?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is quite correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But in your case, you were working with the PJP both in Belgrade and in Kosovo, which suggests that 100 per cent of your time was engaged with the PJP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was sometime on the eve of the war in 1998 that I started working with the police brigade. This unit had a nature that was peculiar and different from all other PJPs. This was the only permanent unit. All the other detachments were ad hoc, set up as needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That clarifies the position, Mr. Ilic. Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Arising out of that, just one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ilic, this PJP detachment in Belgrade that you were a part of, you've already told us that the PJP, itself, was disbanded sometime in, I think, 2001 or thereabouts. This police brigade in Belgrade, does it still exist?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, it still exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you would return from Kosovo to work in the police brigade in Belgrade, this police brigade in Belgrade, what specific tasks in this police brigade in Belgrade did you undertake in between shifts in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR ILIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Securing football matches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does what you've just said mean that the brigade is now part of the gendarmerie, since you indicated yesterday that the PJP had been disbanded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. Back in 2001, the PJP was disbanded but not the brigade. As for the gendarmerie, it was set up independently from the brigade. These are two unrelated units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And just for the avoidance of any doubt, certainly in my mind, prior to 2001, was that police brigade regarded as part of the PJP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was, part of it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ilic. That completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give evidence. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, our next witness is Mr. Gvozden Gagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, before he comes into court, there is one matter that I think Mr. Hannis wants us to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that procedural matter I spoke of just before we recessed last evening; and, actually, Ms. Kravetz is here to present a firmer version of the Prosecution's position than I did last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This matter concerns an outstanding application by the Lukic Defence to add exhibits to the exhibit list for the third witness who is scheduled this week. This is witness Mr. Paponjak. We were requested yesterday by the Legal Officer of the Chamber via e-mail to indicate whether we intended to respond to this motion, and we indicated we would respond orally given that the witness is scheduled either to testify today or tomorrow. Our position and our request to the Chamber is that this motion to add exhibits be denied. The Defence is requesting that 65 exhibits be added to their exhibit list to be tendered through this witness, and they've indicated in this motion that these were exhibits that were provided by the witness in the final preparation for his testimony. These exhibits, in fact, were exhibits that were tendered through this witness's testimony in the Milosevic Defence in May 2005. They have been available and in possession of the Defence now for a number of years, and also the transcript of this testimony has been in their position for some years. This witness is not a new witness, he's been on the Defence witness list since June of 2007, and the Defence have not provided any valid reason why these 69 exhibits were not included in their original exhibit list and are being added at this late stage. I wish to indicate that, out of the 69 exhibits, 32 of them are untranslated. In the Milosevic case, these exhibits were tendered and marked for identification, and translations were requested. It is my understanding that some of the translations were completed. We have no way of tracking which ones have been translated because this was a Defence request at the time, but we have not been provided with any translations for these 32 exhibits. I don't know if the Defence has made any attempts at obtaining these translations. I also wish to add that this witness who's probably either going to testify today or tomorrow has been scheduled as a 92 ter witness. We were provided with his witness statement only yesterday, almost at the end of the session, at 7.00 in the evening. The exhibits that the Defence wishes to add are listed in the witness statement. So, in addition to requesting that the motion be denied, we're requesting that the paragraphs that refer to these statements -- to these exhibits in the witness statement be removed, be stricken out. Those are my submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, is that for you or for Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it's for me. Regarding the exhibits, I think that they were all listed on Thursday, and it's not the first time that the exhibits are listed in this witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's something I don't understand. We're told that there are 69 exhibits which you seek to have added to the 65 ter list, which suggests that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- until that application is made, they're not part of your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is true, it was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As we work on a day-by-day basis, we on Thursday added these exhibits and actually tried to add these exhibits to our list. These documents were really used during the Milosevic trial, so it was not for the Prosecution -- the new knowledge about their existence. So they were -- they knew the witness is coming, the evidence was used during the Milosevic trial. So they were aware that those documents would be used with this witness. It's nothing new for them, so I don't think that it is any kind of ambush. Regarding the translations, we tracked everything we could from the Milosevic trial, and I think the documents that we found are also included in both versions, B/C/S and English. So I don't think that -- I don't see how the Prosecution can be surprised with these documents. And regarding the translation, Mr. Ivetic I think has more data. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as you know, I've been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As you know, I've been the part of the team that's trying to deal with CLSS to get urgent treatment for translations that are urgently required for upcoming witnesses. This statement once obtained in the original B/C/S language, Serbian language, from the witness was submitted to CLSS and was given a priority dead-line for translation. CLSS had advised us that the translation would be completed by yesterday. Unfortunately, the translation did not come to us until late in the afternoon on yesterday rather than the beginning of the business day on yesterday. And as soon as we had the translation -- I mean, we were not complaining about CLSS. We're just giving the facts that once we got it back from CLSS, we sent it forward to the Prosecution. As Your Honours are aware, CLSS has many, many other cases to deal with and has many pending requests even from our team, let alone other cases to deal with. This is a statement of some significant number of pages that they did endeavour to get to us; and, unfortunately, they did get it to us by the dead-line, but later in the day than both perhaps they and we had hoped. That is the reason why the translation of the statement was disclosed to the Prosecution at the time that it was yesterday. That's the only representation I can make with respect to that, that as soon as it was available, it was presented to them. There was no holding back of the statement on our part. It's purely a matter of the amount of work that CLSS has to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When was it presented to CLSS?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Last week Friday, Your Honour, it was presented to CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Now, what's the position about the 32 untranslated documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Those documents are from Milosevic trial as well, so we couldn't track the translations for these -- for those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So they have not even been presented for translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are right, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At the end of last week, you indicated the possibility of arranging for the attendance of other witnesses this week. Are there any other witnesses apart from the one we're about to hear and Paponjak for this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We tried to bring more witnesses, but we are told that they can come only on Wednesday night. So it would be -- would not be possible for us to put anybody on the stand from Wednesday night to -- till Thursday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll proceed now to hear the other witness; and at one of the breaks, we will give further consideration to what's been said and indicate our decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, given this newly arisen situation, while the witness is on his way, we have a talk scheduled for Thursday afternoon between 2.00 and 3.00, and we would like to hold those talks that morning, since it's quite obvious at this point that the Lukic Defence will not be bringing any witnesses. We'll all be on our way by Thursday afternoon, so this will be far easier for us. Please, if possible, try to bear that in mind. I would appreciate that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't rely on it, Mr. Fila, but we will bear it in mind. Mr. Gagic, would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. We have a problem, do we?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. Before we begin, I'd just like to mention that two documents that are listed in the exhibit list for this witness, that is, 6D612 and 6D613, are large documents and are in B/C/S only. 6D612 is about 770 pages long and it's been marked for identification; 6D613 is about 670 pages long. I'm just alerting the Chamber to the fact that we have e-mailed the -- Mr. Lukic, the Defence, to request any specific page references that they would be using if at all with this witness. And just to let you know, we have not received a substantive response yet, and, therefore, it will be problematic for me to cross-examine this witness meaningfully on these documents if they are used with him. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gopalan. Mr. Lukic, can you assist on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think that we used this -- those documents only as references, and we are not -- we won't be using them during the cross -- actually, direct examination of this witness. Those are two cases, Izbica and Pusto Selo cases. So there would be some references during this testimony, but we won't be using the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Both are, as you say, marked for identification, so they are -- or is it only one that's marked?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes, I think only one is marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Only 612?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And we have a problem because for us it's almost not possible to have those translated. Those are two big documents. We'll try to extract some pages in the future, but for now we haven't finished that job yet. But most of these documents are photographs and some post mortem exams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll deal with 613 as and when it arises. As far as 612 is concerned, already marked for identification, then any issue over its final admission will have to be addressed when the translation is presented. Meanwhile, if there are specific parts of either document that you seek to cross-examine on, assuming 613 is at least marked for identification, then you would have to do that today. If in the end it turns out to be impossible for you to address parts of these documents meaningfully, then when the translations are presented, no doubt you will bring that to our attention before we have to decide one way or the other whether to finally admit these documents. Mr. Gagic, I think we've now dealt with the administrative preliminaries. You will now be examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Gagic.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have the binder in front of you, right?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: I'm actually allowed to use it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of course, you are.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please introduce yourself, tell us about your background, tell us about your career briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: My name is Gvozden Gagic, born in 1954 in Serbia, I'm an ethnic Serb, my religion is Orthodox. I reside in Belgrade. I completed my -- the primary and secondary education in Belgrade, then I did my regular military term in Pristina. It took me 16 months to complete that. After that, I began studying. I completed the high police school for the interior, and then I also studied defectology. After completing my studies, I got a job with the Ministry of the Interior back in 1980. First, I worked in the Belgrade secretariat; and then between 1996 -- or as of 1996, I started working with the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia and I worked at the ministry HQ; the ministry building itself, that's what I mean. So this would be a brief overview of my career. After that, I worked on crime prevention with the crime prevention police; and until I retired in January 2006, I did all sorts of different jobs. At the outset, I dealt with property-related crime and junior delinquents. Between 2002 and my retirement, I dealt with murder. I was the chief of the department that dealt with the sex-related offences with the Belgrade SUP and the Ministry of the Interior. As of 2004, early in 2004, I became chief of the department for discovering war crimes at the Ministry of the Interior secretariat in Belgrade, it was a unit fighting organized crime; and in 2006 I eventually retired once I had met all legal requirements for retiring.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have to make short breaks for the transcript. You say that you were head of the department for preventing murder and sex-related offences. Can you please name some crimes that would belong to that group under the criminal code?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Most violent crimes, such as for murder, attempted murder, murder causing public danger, causing general risks, grievous bodily harm, slight bodily harm, and other crimes containing an element of violence; but they are also related to other types of criminal offences, such as those property-related that result in death, for example, robbery, and the like. As for sex-related criminal offences, we're talking about rape, attempted rape, indecent behaviour, committing rape of a minor, cases of sexual abuse. This is the range of sex-related criminal offences that I covered. For the most part, I investigated those.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What exactly was your job in March 1999 when the NATO air-strikes began?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: I headed the department that -- for sex-related crime, and that was with the general crime section of Serbia's MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It seems that there was an overlap. Can you please repeat the name of that.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Department for fighting the murder and sex-related criminal offences, general crime section, crime police administration of Serbia's MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So who headed the crime police administration of Serbia's MUP at the time?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: At the time and after, it was General Dragan Ilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is this -- it is a convenient time for me, Your Honour, if it is for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, we have a break at this time every day. I know you've just started your evidence, but we have to have this break so that everyone can return refreshed. While we have it, would you please leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll see you in about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gagic, may we continue?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your glasses ready?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you go to Kosovo and Metohija before the air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Before the air-strikes, I seldom went to Kosovo and Metohija. Between 1997 and the air-strikes, I was in Kosovo only twice, two days at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us move onto the period after the air-strikes commenced. Were there any problems in the work of the UKP, that is, the department of the crime police, in Kosovo and Metohija, as well as in the area of Serbia as a whole?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were problems with the air-strikes. Initial problems arose caused by the bombings. Neither were the services completely ready to work in wartime conditions, or at least in the conditions that were imposed on us, nor did people have any such experience that could be put to good use in terms of analogy. Therefore, at the very outset, serious issues arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Concerning the difficulties in the work of the UKP, was there a decision made or a regulation put in place in order to resolve those issues?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the air-strikes began and after the first calls began arriving from the department of the crime police, indicating that they were not able to deal with the situation fully, the administration sent an instructional dispatch sent to all secretariats including those in Kosovo and Metohija. I'm trying to say that all secretariats in Serbia proper and in Kosovo and Metohija received that. After that, working groups were set up that toured the organizations in the field trying to interpret that dispatch to the local personnel, so as to enable them to proceed further.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Concerning the implementation of the dispatch, did you -- were you sent to Kosovo and Metohija as well?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: I was, and I was tasked to visit all secretariats in Kosovo and Metohija, to meet various chiefs of secretariats, chiefs of UKPs, and crime police department chiefs, to explain the dispatch to them, and to listen to any problems they might be encountering. The goal was to have a uniform approach all over Serbia when proceeding further in the production of regulation and documents following the work of various bodies of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before you went to Kosovo and Metohija, did you go to any parts of Serbia proper with the same goal?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Before going to Kosovo and Metohija, I visited three secretariats in Serbia itself; the one in Cacak, in Prokuplje, and in Jagodina. I went there alone; whereas, to Kosovo and Metohija, I went with one of the chiefs of the forensics department, so as to be able to provide better instruction in terms of forensic work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was the person from the forensics department?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Zoran Radonjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who ordered you to go to Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: The order was received from General Dragan Ilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was your task as a matter of fact?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: My task was, first and foremost, to ensure that there is uniform conduct in the implementation of the dispatch. All cases had to be registered and all security-related events needed to be reported on, including this new occurrence of NATO aeroplanes dropping bombs. Also, uniform reports were supposed to be submitted, not as template forms but rather in the sense of contents of those reports, as well as any further actions taken following such reports including prosecution when the conditions were such.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned this new occurrence, the NATO bombardment. Can you give us any other example of new types of incidents?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: What we were able to observe and what we took measures against in terms of prevention was the fact that many citizens in large towns were in shelters. By that fact alone their property remained unguarded and it could easily be targeted. During air-raids, most of the citizens were inside the shelters. On top of that, people were amassing goods, including dangerous material such as oil, gas; that is to say, flammable substances that could endanger the life and health of large numbers of groups, especially if we are talking about apartment blocks and so on and so forth. Of course, there were other occurrences as well. We can go into detail a bit later if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was contained in the instructional dispatch of the 29th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: The instructional dispatch contained something that we had noticed before that, and that is that various secretariats and departments of crime police reported in different forms and they were sending reports to the ministry that differed amongst themselves. On occasion, they would write criminal reports or they would submit independent, separate reports. Sometimes, they would send official notes. There was a point at which people could no longer handle that material. That was one of the main reasons to ask for that uniform approach, and that the only difference should be the contents relating to a particular event rather than the presentation of those events. All elements needed for further activity in relation to those cases needed to be ensured, so that prosecutors could use that to prosecute and to turn that material into criminal reports. We asked that all -- that reports be drafted concerning incidents which had to do with the NATO air-strikes. These were the so-called P4 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: PU forms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- which were to accompany forensics reports and on-site investigation reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What does the "PU" stand for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honours, but the witness has mentioned an instructional dispatch of the 29th of March, 1999. I wonder if we could have an exhibit number for the document he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid we don't have that document with us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anything else you want to say on it, Ms. Gopalan?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, what was ordered to authorised police officials to do?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Authorised police officials, when undertaking measures, had to submit reports, as well as all other forms or documents, as they had been doing previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. Except for those forms and the red tape, what else were they supposed to be doing?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: They were ordered to carry out on-site investigations always, of course provided that there is sufficient security for them in the field. They were ordered to inform prosecutors about all events. There was an additional request which had to do with a new way of conducting analyses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to the prosecutor, were they supposed to inform anyone else?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: They had to inform the prosecutor about any particular event, and an investigative judge was supposed to attend the scene; however, they could delegate that to the organs of the Ministry of the Interior for several reasons, of course in keeping with the Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have to adjust the forms to the newly created situation?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: In the initial phase, we were not adjusting or formatting the templates or forms in the sense of the necessary elements that had to be filled out. It was a piece of paper resembling the reports you frequently encounter here concerning security-related events. Later on, because there was an interruption in the chain of informing, a novelty was introduced. Do you want me to explain it right away?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Since there was an interruption in the chain of informing and in communication, most buildings were bombed including the Pristina SUP building containing the switchboard for most of Kosovo and Metohija. Because of that, we could not continually monitor the situation and do any statistics of those security-related events from the area of crime. Before the introduction of the information system, and I mean to say an IT system, we had a classical information system. Those who submitted criminal reports were obliged to fill out the statistical forms or lists. There were three types of lists: One was called KD1 pertaining to crimes, which should contain a description of the crime according to a strictly-prescribed set-up; the second is KD2 relating to perpetrators; and the third is the PU list, that is, a list of events which in themselves need not to be crimes but may be in cases of fires, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hold any meetings in Kosovo and Metohija; and if so, with who?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: In Kosovo and Metohija, I had meetings with the chiefs of crime police, as well as with chiefs concerning general crime and forensics. Sometimes, I wanted to meet them in the field or in Pristina or elsewhere; and, sometimes, I visited them in their offices. I preferred visiting them and holding meetings at their SUP seats, rather than forcing them to come to see me for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Concerning that, did you have any meetings at the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: I did; however, I was using the MUP staff as a facility to hold meetings. At those meetings, there were no MUP staff members until I became a member of the staff. In the initial phase, no one from the MUP staff attended those meetings. I simply used their premises to hold those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in Kosovo and Metohija that time?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: That first time, I spent three days there. I visited all the secretariats, I gave instructions, I heard what they had to say, I recorded the problems, and when I returned to my organizational unit, I reported about the situation as it was on the ground and the activities that I undertook.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In terms of your line of work in the MUP staff, who worked there?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: In my line of work at that time, that is to say, from when the NATO bombing started, Tomislav Blagojevic was there. He's from Krusevac. And when the staff was established, he was sent by the appropriate officers in the relevant period of time to be the assistant for crime for that line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was there in the MUP staff in your line of work before him?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Novica Zdravkovic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have in e-court P1889.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have the exhibit before you, don't you?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What's the date on this document?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: The 30th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: About who?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: This is a decision made by the then-head of the sector, Vlastimir Djordjevic, and it has to do with the decision concerning Lieutenant-Colonel Tomislav Blagojevic, who would no longer be working at the MUP in this line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see when Tomislav Blagojevic was sent to the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: We see that he was sent on the 15th of February, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Blagojevic was injured in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic happened to be in the MUP building when it was bombed, and he sustained light injuries on that occasion; however, the fact that he happened to be in the building that time affected his activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Blagojevic go out into the field after he was injured after the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, he went out into the field rarely. I can say that he practically did not; however, his work in the MUP staff in terms of following crime developments was not really linked to going out into the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see this decision in e-court, and do we see who it was that sent Mr. Blagojevic there and who actually passed this decision?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: I already mentioned Colonel-General Vlastimir Djordjevic, assistant minister, head of the sector public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In relation to this first visit, who did you report to, in relation to this first order, "nalog," on account of which you came to Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: I reported to General Ilic, who had given me the order in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After that, did you get yet another order to go to Kosovo and Metohija; and if so, when and from who?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Throughout the period of the NATO bombing, I often went to Kosovo and Metohija, always on orders from my superior, General Ilic or one of his assistants or one of the chiefs of departments, but mainly it was from Dragan Ilic. The next time I went to Kosovo, this had to do with activities regarding Pusto Selo, activities related to finding a large number of unidentified bodies in the area of Pusto Selo, which is in the region of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know how this first information was obtained concerning the existence of this grave in Pusto Selo?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: The first information came on the basis of satellite imagery that was broadcast. We had not known about the existence of this kind of grave. Later on, we established it wasn't a mass grave in the classical sense of the word mass grave. This had to do with a burial of a larger number of bodies, but we do not know who it was who had buried the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who ordered the exhumation and the post mortems of these bodies?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: It was ordered by the investigating judge of the court that had jurisdiction. It is on his orders that the entire exhumation was conducted by the crime police department, and additional work was done by the workers of the public company from the area of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was your specific role on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Well, since it had to do with a significant number of mortal remains, and in view of the fact that the security situation was a highly complex one, the post mortem had to be carried out as quickly as possible. On that occasion, three institutes were engaged, or rather, four institutes if I include the institute in Pristina; that is to say, the forensic medicine institutes. These are institutions that do not belong to the police system. These are medical institutions.
