It was the forensic medicine institute in Belgrade, the forensic medicine institute in Novi Sad, the forensic medicine institute in Nis, and the forensic medicine institute in Pristina which was the host institute as well. My job was to ensure all necessary logistics for the forensic specialists and physicians, so that they could carry out their work quickly, but of course not to the detriment of quality. On the contrary, they had to work professionally at a high standard but as fast as possible. So I was the logistics man; and in addition to the fact that I provided accommodation and food for them, I also brought in a certain number of bodies from Prizren, which is pretty far away to Pristina, so that they could work at full capacity in a single day, so that there wouldn't be any halts in their work. So I fully met that requirement as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, was everything done in accordance with the ZKP of the SFRY that was in force at that time?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. The ZKP hadn't changed significantly in this respect. All legal requirements were observed and all other rules that are not envisaged by the ZKP, and these are the rules of burial and the like, which was part of the work of the public company involved. So everything was done in accordance with the ZKP and other laws and bylaws.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What does "ZKP" mean? And please tell us what state is involved. I think that there is a mistake.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: The ZKP is the Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it the SFRY or the FRY?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: At that time it was the law of the SFRY, or rather, no, the FRY. Because republics did not have this law, it was the law of the FRY. That was the time of the FRY, so it was the law of the FRY, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of reports were compiled in relation to Pusto Selo?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Two types of report were filed in relation to Pusto Selo. One type of report was of the individual type. It had to do with each and every corpse and had been exhumed. These reports were signed by the expert team that had carried out the post mortems, so that is the post mortem record. And, finally, at the end of the activity concerned, a single report was filed that was signed by all the participants in this process. It was a compilation of all the activities that took place during the course of those six days at the institute of forensic medicine in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you see a document of the Army of Yugoslavia that had to do with clean-up, "asanacija," and could you tell us something about that term, "clean-up," "sanitization."

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: As for this term, "asanacija," I first came across it on that occasion when we were involved in these activities pertaining to Pusto Selo, because this is not a term that is used in police jargon or in police rules; that is to say, in bylaws regulating the work of the police and the laws regulating the work of the police. Indeed, this came as a novelty to me. Since this new term had appeared, and I did not know exactly what it meant and what it involved, first I took measures with a view to familiarizing myself with the term of "asanacija," what it meant during a war; and then I also had occasion to see a document, an order, "naredba," that had been issued by the army in relation to "asanacija," sanitization, by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What's the term that's used in the police or what are the terms used in relation to finding corpses?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: There is no special term that is used within the police in terms of finding a single corpse or several corpses. Quite simply, this is an on-site investigation according to the ZKP. The territory is called the scene. So all these terms that are used in crime investigation are well-known ones, and there are no special terms, let alone "asanacija."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who carries out activities that have to do with finding corpses on the ground?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: In relation to finding corpses on the ground, there is exhumation, or rather, there are investigations that are taken in accordance with the order issued by the investigating police by authorised officers of the crime police. As a rule, a crime police inspector heads the team involved, and the on-site investigation is carried out by a senior crime technician. This rule can be changed as well. So the on-site investigation can be carried out in the absence of an investigating judge if he duly authorises the organ of the interior. Before the on-site investigation, the territorial prosecutor in charge is informed about the activities that would be carried out on his territory; and as a rule, the prosecutor is out on the scene in the case of serious crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to the court and the police that you've already mentioned, are other structures involved, too, on the ground?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Public services of local self government are involved in these activities on the ground. Their task is to secure access to the scene of the occurrence, especially if it is inaccessible. Firefighters can be used if necessary, or rather, if it is necessary to clear the ground, to do away with obstacles if any. But, usually, it is public services that are used for that. However, usually, there aren't many people employed in such services within the local government. So if it is necessary to have more people involved in order to make it possible to reach the scene of the crime as soon as possible, fire-fighting units can be engaged as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, that is to say, during the course of the war, were civilian and military judicial authorities active?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout the NATO aggression and throughout the period of war, both civilian and military organs functioned. I am not familiar with the level of cooperation between these authorities, and I am not aware of their internal jurisdictions, their internal divisions, too, and other subdivisions, but I know that they functioned along parallel lines, both types of authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up in e-court now 6D116. This has to do with 6D613, however, that's a document that has not been translated and that is a lengthy document, but we will just be using this shorter document that I first mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you, while you were in Kosovo and Metohija in May 1999, did you receive any information about the existence of another mass grave?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, yes, now we have it in English, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, please go on.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Towards the end of May and the beginning of July, or rather, at the end of May, again satellite imagery showed a mass grave in the area of Kosovska Mitrovica, in the municipality of Srbica, in the village of Izbica. We hadn't known about this mass grave either. Also, it was not a mass grave in the sense in which that term is used. It was the burial site of several bodies at a particular locality that the competent authorities had not been aware of before that, so that is why it was probably termed as it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Whose satellite imagery was used to find this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were commercial satellites covering the area. This had to do with the NATO air-strikes, and this type of satellite imagery was also being used by foreign TV crews. We used those images, and those images were shown in our media as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So how were you alerted to this site in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The moment word was received about this, it was the task of the crime police and the regular police to use these criteria. Should I go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. Who was it that told you about this site? Which organization?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly which organization, but I think the image was shown on BBC. I can't be positive; however, it may have been CNN. I got my assignment from General Ilic, and the assignment was to establish the facts and circumstances and to take the same sort of steps that I had taken in Pusto Selo, to get a medical team in and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered my question. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please just read paragraph 2, which starts: "On the 2nd of June 1999 ..."

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: "On the 2nd of June, 1999, based on a written order of the court, KRA number 107/99, members of the forensic and PD department of the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP carried out forensic activities necessary to document the scene, mark and transport the bodies, and to observe the external description of the bodies."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you preparing to be involved in the Izbica case?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Having remembered the Pusto Selo experience and how the mechanism that we had devised at the time functioned really well, I started my own preparations in terms of assembling a team of forensic experts. The assignment to find the actual grave was received by people from the Suva Reka -- from the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP department of the crime police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who were you informed by about this?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: The first step I took in order to prepare and to pave the way for the forensic experts was to go and see Dr. Slavisa Dobricanin, who was the director of the forensic medicine institute in Pristina. I wanted to see if there was a realistic opportunity to conduct autopsies of these bodies at their institute. We talked about this, and the next day Professor Dobricanin informed me that he had been informed by the Kosovska Mitrovica investigating judge that there would be no post mortem at the forensic medicine institute in Pristina, rather, there would be an external examination of the bodies on the site itself, and that this would be done by forensic experts from the military medical academy in Belgrade. This also spelled the end of my own involvement because I then went on to inform General Ilic about this. I came across the Izbica case at a later stage in the course of my activities, but we'll probably be discussing this more at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the military medical academy, did you ever receive an autopsy report about Izbica?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Due to the nature of my later work, and this was something that I failed to mention in my introduction today when I introduced myself, I found myself needing documents of this kind. This was a job that I did outside the Ministry of the Interior, and this was work that I did for Serbia's government. I didn't receive the documents at the time. I have never received those documents, as a matter of fact, from the VMAs, the military medical academies, forensic institute. I don't know what the reasons might be for that. I can't say I exerted any pressure on them to deliver those documents because I had assumed that maybe the trial itself was to blame for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You spoke about this kind of procedures followed by the police when bodies are found, dead bodies. What about the standard procedure when bodies are found? Can this be done by a committee, for example, set up by officers from the VJ and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: No, it can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about you during your time in Kosovo and Metohija, did you hold meetings with people from the VJ to discuss what the military liked to term "asanacija," clearing up or cleaning up human remains?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: I certainly had no formal meetings about this, about what they call "asanacija," not a single one, not with the VJ or any other bodies for that matter. There was something, however, that could possibly come under this heading, and I mean the use of this military term. I was in touch once with an officer of the VJ, and this had to do with the information suggesting that quite a large number of bodies had been found. It later turned out that this information was not entirely consistent with the situation that I found when I arrived at the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the name of that VJ officer that you talked to?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Hasan Cizmic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Corovic?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're right. I apologise, Hasan Corovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Mr. Corbic complain to you in a way about the police trying to shift the blame to the VJ?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: That wasn't something that we talked about. I wasn't adamant myself that those issues should be discussed. My only specific mission was to verify this particular piece of information about Glogovac, the Glogovac area, and there being quite a large number of human remains there. I ascertained at one point that this information was partly true, and then I got in touch with this gentleman who was in charge of the clean-up, or the "asanacija," as the military say. We agreed that he would be taking additional steps about this, and that's where my involvement ended. Danica Marinkovic, the investigating judge, was there for the final part of our talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's try to get the name right. This must be the third time. The first time it was our mistake, and the second time it was misrecorded. What was the name of this gentleman from the VJ?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Hasan Corbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's fine now. Did you perhaps hear at the time that there were proposals to set up a joint committee of the VJ and the police?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: No, I heard no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A hypothetical question: Say, for example, a joint committee of the VJ and the police, the MUP, was set up, could it possibly take over the powers of the investigating judge in all the other bodies normally involved in a procedure like this?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: First of all, under the law, no such committee could possibly have been established. Secondly, given the extent of the area to be covered by such a committee and given the number of different events that it would be covering, the committee would have had to comprise several hundred persons; and given who was involved at the time, no such committee could possibly have been set up. A body could perhaps have been set up in order to monitor the situation in terms of passing on information of what was going on, but certainly not a committee in charge of conducting the entire procedure from the time the bodies were found to the post mortem. Something like that would have been entirely inconceivable.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could a committee like that have taken over the -- have assumed the powers of an investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: No, not under the law that applied at the time, unless there was an investigating judge, of course, who was a member of that committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We heard that at the staff there were persons who shared your line of work, and we heard who those persons were. What was their role, the role, for example, of Mr. Zdravkovic or that of Mr. Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: I can only talk about Mr. Blagojevic's role because the situation was quite peculiar. Mr. Zdravkovic worked under peacetime conditions, as it were; therefore, I can't vouch for anything I might say about him. But about Mr. Blagojevic, for as long as the war went on, his role - the state of war, I mean - his role was to collect intelligence by cooperating with the crime police department or chiefs in charge of certain types of crime, general crime, white-collar crime. They were to discuss their respective situations in their areas regarding crime. He was also to send reports to the crime police on a daily, weekly, and monthly basis. He was an operative, and most of his work had to do with the area in which the HQ was located. He didn't go out much. He certainly went to no on-site investigations or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the staff or someone from the staff, did they have the power to order you anything?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your time in Kosovo and Metohija and until the 1st of June, 1999, did you have any responsibility towards the leader of that staff, Sreten Lukic?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Not towards Sreten Lukic, not towards any other member of that staff, no responsibility whatsoever. The only commitment that I did have in my own line of work was to report to whichever official was in charge of crime. When I say "commitment," this isn't something that I'd been specifically ordered to do; I mean, to get in touch with them. Sometimes I was in Kosovo without necessarily talking to that officer. It wasn't from Pristina; it was from a different place. When I say "commitment," what I mean is a commitment in terms of exchanging information with this person or another member of the staff, information concerning the security situation along roads that I was expected to be travelling, in order to avoid any danger to my own life or those of other passengers and in order to ensure that my task would be carried out in a timely manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Blagojevic, did he have the power to order anything to the UKPs of the SUPs in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: No. He couldn't order any tasks to be executed. He could only pass along orders that he had received from the UKP in Belgrade, in a purely technical sense. The MUP headquarters in Belgrade had no communications. For the most part or throughout most of the period we are talking about, it had no direct communication with the SUPs because the communications systems had been damaged or disrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that General Dragan Ilic held meetings in Kosovo and Metohija during the air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that General Ilic visited Kosovo and Metohija during the air-strikes. There was this one time he was spending some time in Kosovo and Metohija, and we saw a lot of each other during that period. I know he was meeting chiefs of the UKP and I assume chiefs of the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have Exhibit D1596 [as interpreted] -- P1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, this is a record, rather, minutes of a meeting held of the MUP staff dated the 7th of May, 1999. Do you know that accompanying General Ilic in Kosovo and Metohija were also chief of the KTC Aleksic and sector chief, Sinisa Spanovic, in the first days of May?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I know about that and I saw them at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 1 clearly shows that at number 2, right, of this document, right?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain what "KTC" stands for? That's the first thing?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: "KTC" means criminal technician centre. This is a seat of the criminal technician centre in Belgrade, and they are in the MUP building. They carry out on-site investigations. There is a centre that deals with forensic investigations. It's also a centre that deals with the technical aspect of any investigation. They collect and secure evidence, any evidence found, and they also do DNA analysis. They started that recently. They don't deal with operative technology, meaning interception devices or anything like that. These are the SOCOs. They deal with analysing crime scenes and taking all the technical steps normally taken during an investigation or an inspection of a crime scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sinisa Spanovic was chief of the search sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my question was not recorded since I forgot to switch my microphone on. The question was: What was Mr. Spanovic's job? Then you answered the question. Thank you. What was the job of this department?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: The search department searches for perpetrators of crimes irrespective of whether a search was initiated by the police or by any of the courts. They also search for objects as well as persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us please go to page 8. I wanted to ask you this: Did you know that the chief of the administration of crime police, General Ilic, held meetings with chiefs of crime police departments in Kosovo and Metohija in early May?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. I know that the chief of the UKP, General Ilic, held a meeting in early May with chiefs of the crime police; that is, chiefs of the various UKPs. However, I did not attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see that from the first bullet point when Major-General Ilic Dragan is addressing the meeting on the 5th of May?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 5th of May at the SUP seat, a meeting was held with the chiefs in Kosovo and Metohija providing further guide-lines for the work of the crime police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you attend the meeting described by General Ilic here?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: I did not attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What can be seen from the bullet point number 2? What information did General Ilic pass on at this MUP staff meeting?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: The tasks were clearly defined with the assessment of the MUP that measures were undertaken; however, insufficient efficiency was achieved in prosecuting all types of perpetrators in the area of K and M. Simply put, it would mean that all measures were undertaken, as well as additional activities that we had to apply because of the newly created situation, in order to improve the work and methods used; however, but that we were still dissatisfied with the results in Kosovo and Metohija. There were many reasons for that, most of which were objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Bullet points 4 and 7, please, read that to yourself.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did General Ilic devise the plan to sanitize the terrain?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: From this document, one would conclude so; however, I did not see the plan. In certain aspects, it resembles "asanacija," but I am unable to provide any further explanation of the two terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did General Ilic tour the SUPs in Kosovo and Metohija in May 1999?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. He visited all SUPs in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the staff created any plans to sanitize the terrain?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with any such documents. Had it been in existence, I probably would have known about it because later I became a member of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please bring up 6D1054 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have that in your binder if it's ease why are for you to have a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: I find it easy enough to read from the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, I'm kindly asking you to find that hard copy because we'll have to move onto page 2. What kind of a document is this?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: The title is, "Order for official travel," and that's precisely what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was the order issued to?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: It was issued to General Dragan Ilic, chief of the UKP of the Republic of Serbia on the 23rd of May, 1999. He was supposed to travel on that day to Pristina. It was issued by an authorised superior, this being Vlastimir Djordjevic, the sector chief in terms of hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 2 that is on the screen, can you tell us from between what dates General Ilic stayed in Kosovo? Can we see that?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: In the upper left-hand corner, we can see the figures the 23rd of May at 700 hours; and just below, it says the 1st of June at 2000 hours. The first date is the day and hour of departure, and the second one is day and time of return. From the rest of the text, one concludes that Dragan Ilic spent ten days in Kosovo and Metohija. Per diem, at the time, was 96 dinars --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right, all right. We can read these details. Come on, Mr. Lukic, let's control the witness and deal with things we need to deal with. All he needed to tell us about this was whether it looked genuine or not, then we can read the rest for ourselves. It's an expenses claim, for goodness sake.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For our case, it's crucial to prove that this gentleman spent ten days at that time in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, all we have is his expenses claim. Bring him to tell us, if you want, but that's his expenses claim. That's as far as it goes. That's all the witness is doing, reading out his expenses claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, do you know whether Dragan Ilic was, indeed, in Kosovo and Metohija at the time?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: I do know that he was in Kosovo; however, we did not meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what tasks he performed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How do you know he was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I do because I had conversations with the chiefs of crime police with whom I had contacts before that and after that. Indirectly, I found out he was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Give me one second, please. [Interpretation] Could we please have Exhibit P1811 brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the exhibit, I wanted to ask you this: Were you sent to Kosovo and Metohija as a MUP staff member; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: I was sent to Kosovo and Metohija to be a member of the staff as of the 1st of January -- excuse me, the 1st of June, 1999, following a decision dated the 31st of May, 1999, signed by Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were in Kosovo and Metohija, before you became a staff member during 1999, did you ever see Radoslav Djinovic at the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it Radoslav?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, Radoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know him otherwise?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know him well. We worked together before the Kosovo events and all the way up to my retirement. We had intensive contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the period when you were a member of the staff. What was the focus of your engagement and the engagement of the staff after you became its member?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: I spent only a brief period of time as a member of the staff in its -- in that current composition. The period lasted for only 20 days. Ten days after the new composition of the staff was introduced, the Military Technical Agreement was signed, preceded by a UN security resolution number 1244. My focal tasks were to organize the withdrawal from Kosovo and Metohija as envisaged by the technical military agreement. At a certain point, all workers of the Ministry of the Interior, as well as the army, were supposed to leave Kosovo and Metohija. Mostly, I dealt with organizational preparation, and we began being active since it was the time of Izbica when I worked on the preparation; and, after that, the Izbica situation was no longer dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mean it was dealt with by someone else?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us please have a look at 6D475 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have that before you?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, prior to the withdrawal of the Yugoslav Serb forces from Kosovo, were you sent to any towns in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was sent, following a meeting in Pristina, where we were briefed and told that in the area of Pec, the security situation is becoming more complex, especially after the Military Technical Agreement had been signed and the resolution put into force, to Pec to see what it was all about and what the degree of complexity is. I was there to try, based on my knowledge and experience, to suggest measures to improve the situation in terms of security, and I was provided -- supposed to provide feedback.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On this document, in the heading, it says: "The staff of the ministry," the date is the 13th of June, 1999. Whose name can be found in the signature block?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Assistant Minister Lieutenant-General Obrad Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, you were a member of the staff?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Mr. Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that later using the MUP staff address for documents. Do you know of any other instances when documents or dispatches are being or were being sent from the staff by people who were not members to the staff; however, in the heading, we still had ministry staff?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know of such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Upon your return from Kosovo and Metohija, what body was formed?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: After return from Kosovo and Metohija in mid-July 1999, two bodies were formed: One was called commission for the implementation or application of the Military Technical Agreement; and the second one was the seat of the staff of KiM, in short APKiM. Its seat was in Kursumlija. The former body met occasionally only; whereas, logistics was located in different places. In the work of the commission, representatives of several different institutions took part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was appointed the head of staff that you mention here?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: The head of the staff was the then-Colonel Dragan Bozovic; he passed away.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have a role on this staff?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, I was the one and only assistant, and later on I was one of the assistants. My line of work was crime investigation because crime went up during the course of a few months.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did this staff deal with missing persons?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was any other body dealing with missing persons?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The secretariats that were dislocated in different localities in Serbia, and this staff was doing that, too. In addition to that, all other secretariats had the obligation to receive records and to take eye-witness statements or family member statements, and then this would be sent by the secretariat to the staff and, of course, to UNMIK.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, did you cooperate with UNMIK in terms of dealing with missing persons?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: This commission for the implementation of the Military Technical Agreement had several components. One of the important ones was a subcommission that dealt with the question of missing persons only. On it were representatives of UNMIK. I was there, or rather, the representatives of the Serbian side, and of the ICRC, the International Committee of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you went from -- to Kosovo and Metohija from time to time, and after you became a member of the staff, did you have any knowledge about alleged crimes, those alleged in the indictment and especially murders? We have looked at the indictment.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't have any knowledge about that. I only knew what was being done in relation to Pusto Selo and Izbica. I did not have any other knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know, for example, about the people who were buried in Izbica? Did they die in fighting or was their death due to crimes committed against them?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: I told you I never got any records from Izbica, but now I'm not dealing with investigations and things like that. I'm not dealing with the prosecution of war crimes. I am in a different line of work, so that is not that meaningful for me now. I cannot talk about what the injuries sustained were, and I cannot claim that if somebody was injured by a fire-arm that this necessarily means a crime. It doesn't rule out that possibility, but anyway that is for forensic experts to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know anything about the transport of bodies from Kosovo and Metohija to Serbia proper?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was it that you first heard of this?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: The first time I heard of this was when it was published in the media; and, also, the Ministry of the Interior acted in order to reveal these facts to find the locations, to carry out exhumations, identification of corpses, corpse inspections, and so on. Then, later on, when mortal remains were handed over, then I participated in that personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, the public security sector, did it take all measures and was their intention serious to find out everything in relation to the bodies that had been found?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: As for the public security sector and the police in general, and as a matter of fact all other organs not only of the police, indeed all necessary measures were taken in order to deal with this professionally, efficiently, fast, and in a humane way. Also, about 800 bodies were found in these locations and 760 were identified. This kind of percentage was never recorded in any war conflict at international level. So the quality of work was professional, at a high level, and timely as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in the work of the operative team for cooperation with The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the Law on Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal was passed, and after the ministries that were duty-bound to cooperate with The Hague Tribunal were designated, every ministry set up a working body of its own. We called ours the operative team for cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, and I took part in its work from the very outset. I did not work there until the end because actually this body never became defunct formally, but it did stop working probably because there was no further need for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was the head of this?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: The head of the operative team was Dragan Furdulovic, the then-head of the division for the investigation of war crimes in the MUP of Serbia; and, at the moment, when I became head of this division and when Dragan Furdulovic was transferred elsewhere, I launched several initiatives to change the head of the operative team because, objectively speaking, he could no longer deal with this work. But the head of team was never changed and, therefore, the body became defunct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Just to note, Your Honours, that the witness's involvement in the operative team for the cooperation with The Hague Tribunal I don't believe is listed in his 65 ter summary as an area that he would testify to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are checking this, Your Honour. But I can move on anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that it's an appropriate time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have much longer?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, not actually. Probably another -- less than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. We'll break now. Mr. Gagic, we have to have another break, for half an hour this time. Please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we shall resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gagic, can we?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please give me answers that are as brief as possible so that we finish as soon as possible. Do you remember interviewing Bozidar Protic?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do remember that I conducted an interview with Bozidar Protic in relation to his testimony, when he was summoned to testify before the Hague Tribunal. Before that, he had already been interviewed in the MUP concerning his knowledge about mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Protic tell you, officially or unofficially, that when he went to Kosovo and Metohija, in order to transport the corpses, he made telephone contact with someone in Pristina who he then thought was Sreten Lukic?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to note, again, that Mr. Protic's testimony is not mentioned in the 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see that. Are you taking any point about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes, I am, to the extent that I would not have had the opportunity to prepare to cross-examine the witness on this area of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give me an indication of what you might have done, because we've recently had this very issue explored in some very detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: That may be the case, Your Honour. But in terms of specific steps I would have taken, if I had advanced notification, for example, would have been listing exhibits that relate to Mr. Protic, to have familiarized myself with his testimony given during the Prosecution case. While the issue might have been addressed with other witnesses in the course of this trial during the Defence case, I would have certainly have reviewed the material in detail if I had advance notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Why was notice not given, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I saw that the Exhibit Number P586 is on the list of the Prosecutor and that's Protic's statement given to this group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. But the issue at the moment is why there's no reference to this in your 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The reason just yesterday or the day before in the conversation with this witness, and I'm finished with this topic. I'm not going to dwell on it anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Just give us a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this could have caused real difficulty, but because the witness is likely to be here tomorrow and because the subject is so well-known and has been explored recently, and, therefore, the Prosecution are in a position to prepare themselves for tomorrow we will not insist on disregarding that evidence. At the same time, we would encourage you to be clear in these 65 ter lists, even to the point of seeking revisal to the notice in relation to a witness where a particular issue is going to be addressed that's clearly of importance in the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell us, just in a few words, about the bodies that you took part in after the signing of the Military Technical Agreement?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: As I've already mentioned, I worked in this commission for the implementation of the Military Technical Agreement, where I cooperated with KFOR and UNMIK. After that, I actively participated in the work of the coordination centre for Kosovo and Metohija, where I led the bureau for missing persons. I also worked on the commission of the state union of Serbia and Montenegro for missing persons pertaining to the entire territory of the former Yugoslavia. For three years, I was also chairman of that commission. Now that is the commission of the Republic of Serbia for missing persons, and I am an advisor to the chairman of that commission, Veljko Odalovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you and organizations that you cooperated with interested in working on uncovering crimes committed in the relevant period of time?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: The activity of these organizations and the degree of their interest was very low. I state that with full responsibility because from the very moment I started cooperating with these organizations, I am primarily referring to KFOR and UNMIK, we lost a lot of time over legal and administrative rules that we were trying to adopt rather than dealing with the subject matter itself. What is characteristic and atypical is that KFOR made a one-sided decision to exclude the safety of citizens in Kosovo and Metohija from the province of work of this commission. Quite simply, they wanted to disband that part of the team for cooperation, so he did not want -- they did not want UNMIK or us to take part in the further work of this body. At our initiative after this decision taken by KFOR, we were compelled to speed things up and to set up a new body to cooperate with UNMIK. That was the committee for police cooperation on the basis of a protocol on cooperation that was signed, and it was based on that. It is in function to the present day, but not entirely because the subject I deal with, missing persons, was transferred to this commission for missing persons that I spoke of earlier. Also, with regard to the uncovering of crimes, UNMIK and KFOR expressed no interest whatsoever in what was going on before they arrived. However, their interest was low, so I think that we managed only on one occasion, in the case of the killing of the family Stolic from Obilic, we managed to set up a joint team that worked on the uncovering of this crime, this murder. Thanks to our crime policemen, evidence was found in terms of the commission of this crime. Regrettably, the perpetrators have not been prosecuted yet. The same situation occurred in relation to the documentation that we submitted to them, and this has to do with a case that we call the severed heads. A group of Albanians can be seen in a photograph, and they are holding in their hands severed heads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: My apologies for interrupting again, Your Honours. Just to note that the work of the commission for missing people was not mentioned in the 65 ter summary. I didn't mention it earlier on in the -- during the witness's testimony because it seemed to me that the question could have been answered in a yes and no manner. This is at line 72, 10. However, the witness has been speaking about this commission for quite a while now, and, therefore, I just wanted to draw the Court's attention to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, there's no sign of this in your 65 ter summary either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will move on then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Working within their UKP, which is something that we gave notice about, did you take part in the arrest of a group that was colloquially referred to as the Skorpions; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: As head of the department for the uncovering of war crimes, in 2005, I took part in the arrest of the group called Skorpions. I am duty bound to say that this is a group that committed crimes in Bosnia-Hercegovina. This is a well-known group, the Skorpions. The case is that of Treskavica, the killing of several civilians in relation to Srebrenica. In relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please stop there. You were asked if you had taken part in the arrest; and if so, when. I don't think it's of relevance to our case that there was an arrest in Bosnia. If you were involved in arresting them in relation to Kosovo, please tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask you about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The persons arrested on account of crimes committed in the area of Srebrenica, were they the persons who committed the crimes in Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which was the unit that was in Podujevo, the members of which committed murders in 1999?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: That was the SAJ reserve unit, colloquially known as the Skorpions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have P1188.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have the document in front of you, don't you?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What's this dispatch about? There are two, as a matter of fact, right?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is an amendment to a previous dispatch. One is a dispatch and the other one is an amendment or a modification of the previous one. The chief of crime police of Kosovo secretariat is here being called to a meeting in order to bring documents, and the documents are specified in this dispatch and other forms of consultation as well. Who drew this up?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this still on the subject of the Skorpions?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we haven't the answer to whether this witness was involved in arresting them or not, and when. We've lost sight of that, have we?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you instructed us to leave the subject if it's -- this arrest is not connected with Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. So he wasn't involved in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You drew up this dispatch. Why are you sending this dispatch to anyone?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: This was a perfectly regular way to communicate with the chiefs of the crime police whenever we needed to meet or agree any further activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What's the amendment about?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: The previous dispatch, at the second-to-last item, talks about the overall number of bodies found, how they were recorded, gender, age, that sort of thing. The amendment was about documents being forwarded in relation to unidentified identicals. That being the only amendment, it wasn't necessary to forward documents about all the bodies found, but rather those unidentified alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What does the header say and what does the date seem to be?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: MUP of the Republic of Serbia, MUP staff, the 28th of May, 1999, Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the signature line?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: This is not the original copy and the signature reads, "Distributed from the staff," but normally you find the signature of whichever operator produced the electronic copy. The original contains the signature of the head of staff, Sreten Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you at the time a member of the staff?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why are you sending this dispatch from the staff? We see the MUP staff in the signature line. You claim that Sreten Lukic's signature was on the document as well.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Just a small correction. We see my signature on the document, but the typed-up version read Sreten Lukic, just as the header was made, and then the head of staff was actually Sreten Lukic. But the signature is mine, and it has the word "for" right in front of it because I used both. I'm sending a dispatch, although I'm no staff member, no member of the staff at the time, because this was a way of communicating. Say, for example, I'm somewhere in Kosovo, I'm in a position where I need to send someone a document, any kind of document, somewhere in Kosovo and Metohija to do with my line of work, my line of work being the work of the crime police. I have to use the number that belongs to my administration, and I have to send this dispatch from the seat of the ministry. Since I am out in the field, I use the staff instead. It is on behalf of the staff that I call this meeting, but I hold this meeting on behalf of the crime police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we look at the document we see that there is a reference and it reads: "Pursuant to PU and KU ..." Are these the forms that we discussed earlier on and that you modified?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are the forms that I established and I modified the forms. I tailored them to suit the needs of this war situation. I envisaged all the categories, perpetrators being active-duty military officers or member of the police and that sort of thing, because the earlier forms had none of that. So, as I said, these are the very forms that I had ordered to be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we see the signature? At the moment I'm not, I'm afraid, following this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a dispatch, so there is no signature on this type of document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what's the reference, then, to signature that you've just been asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The witness just expanded his answer, telling us that there was a document on which he is aware about existing -- existence of his signature, but we don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is an answer: "The original contains the signature of the head of staff, Sreten Lukic."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked whether there was, but I was corrected by the witness that there was his signature on that; only the name was of the Sreten Lukic, typed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Clarify this a little. You said, and I don't know what was recorded, when you signed documents, you would put a word right in front of the signature?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, "for" or "on behalf," and I used both in the case of this particular dispatch. As far as I remember, I used the word "for."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean you were signing it on behalf of Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. I still don't understand then, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I signed this dispatch in my own name; however, I'm dispatching it from the staff for the sake of completeness in terms of procedure because I'm now in Kosovo. I should go to Belgrade to send this dispatch, again it must be sent to Pristina to the staff, and then be distributed to the secretariats. I am taking a shortcut here. I am in the staff; from there, I send it to chiefs of the UKP across the secretariats; I sign the dispatch in front of the name and surname that is already typed up in the document, just as the header is. It is at the bottom of the, page in this and other documents, that you find the signatory, the head of staff, and then I put my signature there, so that whoever receives a dispatch knows I was the one who sent it from the staff and that I was the one calling the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just have to make one correction. The page numbers are mixed up now, but I think it's page 73, line 18. There is an answer of this witness recorded as my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For some reason, my transcript's now back on single numbers-

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Same with us, so that's page number 1, then, line 18: "This is an amendment to the previous dispatch." It's the answer of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the answer is both 17 and 18 to 22?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These standardised forms that you asked to be delivered in this dispatch, when did you forward them to the UKPs across Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: It was sometime in early May, between the 5th and the 10th of May. I gave them a generous dead-line to enter all the different kinds of information, to process any information that they had by the 25th of May, and that was the period to be covered and that was the period that we were interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 6D874 brought up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is the last document in your binder, sir. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What does the header say?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Again, ministry staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the date?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: The 6th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did you find out about this letter?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: I found out about this circular because, to some extent, I was myself involved in the sense of me being the person who put it together along with Spanovic. Then we gave it to General Ilic, who then entered certain corrections, changed a number of terms that were used in the original. There were a few corrections to be made. Then, in my presence, he signed it and had it distributed to all the parties involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whose name do we see typed up at the end of this document?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: As in the previous case, and this was a general rule, head of staff Major Sreten Lukic, and it was subsequently signed by whoever happened to be sending the circular out. Any recipients would know that this is the person informing them and this is the person who is sharing information with them. So the situation is perfectly identical. It's just that the header that was used was the header of the MUP staff. The fact is that General Ilic was in Kosovo at the time, and this was to keep him from going back to Belgrade just because of a single document and then going back to Kosovo, because this was the mechanism that was in place at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we go to the end of the document, please, in both English and B/C/S, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we look at the Serbian, there is no signature. This is the copy we're looking at. At the time the document was produced, did you see General Ilic's signature?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what I said a while ago. He entered certain corrections, he signed the document, and then he had it distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Gagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the time being this concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will deal with a particular issue. I started with Veljko Odalovic, he was my witness, and I'm going to press on with Mr. Gagic now. You know, at 3.4 of the indictment, killings, paragraph 75 at 2 is the only reference to the 300 persons. I think this is an issue that has been greatly neglected in the work before this Chamber, and I hope to have an opportunity to shed some light on this matter with the assistance of Mr. Gagic. The most dangerous category is when someone who went missing. We who went through the war know exactly what this means. It was very difficult in Kosovo, and it was very difficult for us to ascertain those who were missing were dead. There were a few cases where they survived and were eventually found. What I'm trying to say is Mr. Gagic told us about who was involved on behalf of the state, UNMIK and the Kosovo group Albanians who deal with this, Odalovic from this side. And what I'm trying to say also a number of NGOs contributed greatly to this process, the Humanitarian Rights Foundation, the Natasa Kandic people and others, and the situation we have today is much, much better fortunately. I'm sorry for talking about this at such great length. I am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, the reference you've given, paragraph 75?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] (H), (H).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gagic, I gave quite a speech; but for that reason, I don't need to keep you for so long.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Fila please be asked to speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What appears to be the situation today in March 2008, how many missing persons from the two ethnic groups and then later on moving onto something else?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: We have a consolidated list, a verified list, that was accepted by both the Albanian side and us, and international organizations as well, and I mean the ICRC. The figure given there is 1-9-7-2, 1.972 persons, about 1.500 Albanians, and the rest were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can I, therefore, conclude that this list is a work in progress in a manner of speaking because you're trying to get the facts straight one way or the other and to finalise this process?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. By all means, this is a dynamic list. It waxes and wanes, in a manner of speaking, from time to time, and it is looked at anew each three months. I have a list here from June last year, and the figure was over 2.000. If necessary, I can refer to the list or I can hand it over to the Chamber or to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'd rather bide my time and see if Odalovic can hand it over, to me at the end of this trial and see how definitive a list that is, and then I will hand over to the Chamber. Tell me this, Count (H) of the indictment, the Prosecutor claims that 300 people went missing in Meja, seven of them having been found killed. This is something that you did in Batajnica - yeah right, that's what I think - and some others, too. Do you know anything about the 300 persons from Meja who went missing?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: I only encountered this in 2001. I wasn't aware of it at the time during my time in Kosovo. It was at a later stage that I came across this when I dealt with the documents for the register of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the fate of 300 persons, if you can.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: I am sorry. About this, there is nothing I can say about the fate of 300 persons because in order to ascertain that, I would need to have records. I would need to have access to UNMIK records. Based on this, it's very difficult for me to say how many persons UNMIK actually identified, how many bodies they identified in Kosovo, how many bodies they handed over to their families. As far as our side is concerned, I conducted no analysis, not based on those criteria. I did not study individual cases. It was based on territorial distinctions that I conducted analysis. For your information, most of those missing were from the Djakovica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all from me, Your Honour. Perhaps you want to delve deeper into this, but I have nothing further to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I thank you and all of those who assisted you in reaching those figures and conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gagic, good afternoon. My name is Djuro Cepic, and I appear on behalf of Mr. Lazarevic. I have but a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the first question, could we please see P1989 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for it, Mr. Gagic, I wanted to tell you what the topic will be, and that is a discrepancy in terms. You mentioned General Ilic who mentioned the word "saniranje," of the terrain, as opposed to the term "asanacija."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: "Saniranje" can be conditionally interpreted as "restoring the terrain."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We have before us the minutes of a meeting at the MUP staff dated the 4th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to page 4 in both versions. The third, not the fourth. [In English] Third page, please, also in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, if you look at the bottom of the page. We can see, among other bullet points of item 2, the fourth one refers to "asanacija" of the battle-field. Can you tell me something about the difference between the terms "saniranje," of the terrain, or "asanacija," of the battle-field. Is it the same or different?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Since I had to learn what "asanacija" means, since I mentioned it in my previous testimony, I can tell you that "saniranje" is one thing and "asanacija" another. I cannot equate the two activities, since in the first military term there is a mention of a battle-field. The second term refers to terrain. For the MUP, we meant the terrain of the entire Kosovo; whereas, in military terms, a battle-field is limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Technically speaking, on the 4th of April, already there is "asanacija" mentioned. You described some of your activities during that time. You will agree that the term "asanacija" was used by the MUP at the beginning of the state of war, was it not?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: It is possible at the beginning of the war. If it was used indeed, it was used in officer communication, in communication between officers who had completed the military academy, who knew of the term. It was not used by other MUP members since it was a term we were not familiar with. I didn't know of it until the end of April, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Concerning the difference between "saniranje," of a territory, and "asanacija," for example, when a human corpse, is found is the procedure always the same? First we need an order of an investigative judge and all the other activities you specified. Is it in both situations like that?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Law on Criminal Procedure is applied in both cases. In military terminology and tasks, we have the military investigative judge of course. When the military organs are dealing with it, they -- their own investigative judge appears as opposed to the civilian district court who have geographical jurisdiction, territorial jurisdiction, over the territory where the remains had been found.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: To go back to Izbica, we saw that some activities were undertaken in order to shed light on the events, and that was done by the district court in Kosovska Mitrovica. You will agree with me that in keeping with the Law on Criminal Procedure, that court and all other courts is independent in terms of their decision as to who will do the expert analysis?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is completely up to them what institution or institute they will turn to.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that that freedom on their part existed in 1999 as it exists today. A competent judge, on his orders, chooses any and all relevant bodies that are to undertake any activities?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, what was the answer to your last question?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: The answer is yes, the competent judge is completely free to choose the institution or body to carry out autopsies or any other activities pertaining to the mortal remains that had been found.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Gagic, I am pausing for the transcript. You will agree with me as well, I believe, that the expert carrying out that analysis is duty-bound to forward his findings and reports only to the judge who had issued an order for him to do so?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the expert's obligation when he completes his analysis, including additional analyses. Such reports, as a rule, are not drafted immediately, but after a short while because there might be additional analyses in terms of toxins and so on and so forth. It can take up to a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The focal point in studying the file any further is the competent court, and the MUP or any other bodies can act only following a request made by the judge or the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: The prosecutor is the main person in charge, and the police can independently undertake certain activities of their own; whereas, for some other activities, they have to have an agreement on the part of the prosecutor or the judge if it involves investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The last question: Concerning those severed heads, it resounded throughout the Serbian public. Can you tell us what specifically it entailed?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: I took part from beginning to end of that issue. There was a photograph, and an expert assessed it is a true original. There are eight Albanians in the photograph, some in uniform, some without, holding severed heads in their hands. Next to them was a bag containing other heads, most likely. That photograph was taken during the conflict in Kosovo and Metohija. It was published in the media. After that, I initiated measures in order to ascertain the identity of persons in the photograph, as well as the identity of those severed heads. Out of the eight people in the photograph, five were identified. The deceased were not identified; although, there are certain indicators as to their identity. We handed over the entire file towards the end of 2004 to UNMIK; and then, again, through the war crimes prosecutor of Serbia, we handed that material over to Mr. Hartman who was the prosecutor of this Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In Kosovo. The witness will have to repeat the end of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you repeat the very end of your answer, please. There was some confusion after the reference to Mr. Hartman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The case file was handed over to Mr. Hartman, since the identifiers had been -- the perpetrators had been identified and the photograph was assessed to be the original. The perpetrators were not brought in, they were in the processed; although, I know that one of them still works for the Kosovo police force and another person works for the Kosovo protection force.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: These are all former KLA members?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave, our Defence team, in keeping with the law -- the request to supplement the exhibit list, submitted that motion. I don't know whether Mr. Hannis objected to that, and I don't know whether that objection still stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not following you, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to be as specific as possible. We submitted a request in line with Rule 65 ter. We asked for two photographs with severed heads to be admitted into evidence. These are the photographs that Mr. Gagic has explained just now. At that point, the Prosecutor objected to the admission of these photographs. So my question is primarily addressed to Mr. Hannis, whether he still objects to having them perhaps admitted into evidence or having them placed -- this photograph placed on the list of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. What was the Trial Chamber's decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our proposal was refused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that's where matters rest. Photographs add nothing to the information we've just been given, Mr. Cepic. There's no need to review or revisit that situation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, we will have to terminate our proceedings for the day shortly, and your evidence will resume tomorrow, that will be at 9.00 tomorrow morning in this courtroom. Meanwhile, between now and then, it is vital that you have no communication with anyone at all about any aspect of the evidence in this case, not just your evidence, anybody's evidence in this case. So please bear that in mind and now please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I will now deal with the debate we had earlier in relation to the 65 ter exhibit list and the Rule 92 ter statement relating to the evidence of Radovan Paponjak. On the 13th of March, the Lukic Defence asked the Chamber to add 69 exhibits to the Rule 65 ter list on the basis that Paponjak had brought these documents with him to The Hague and that -- and thus the Lukic Defence had been unaware of them. The Lukic Defence has also moved under Rule 92 ter for the admission of part of the evidence of the witness by way of written statement. The Prosecution object to the amendment of the exhibit list on the basis that the Lukic Defence should have known about these documents because they featured in the Milosevic case, and moreover 32 of the 69 documents are not translated. The Prosecution also object to the late intimation of the Rule 92 ter statement; however, rather than ask for it all to be rejected, it only asks the Chamber to disregard those portions of the statement that discuss these documents. In response to that, the Lukic Defence say that the documents were known to the Prosecution for the very reason that they were tendered in the Milosevic case. The Lukic Defence also argue that they tracked as many of the documents as it could and disclosed the ones that were translated to the Prosecution, but have not submitted the untranslated ones for translation yet. And, finally, they submit that the Rule 92 ter statement was submitted to CLSS last week for translation and was disclosed to the Prosecution as soon as possible, which was yesterday afternoon. In passing, I remark that we are all extremely grateful to CLSS for producing a translation of such a lengthy statement so quickly. And, Mr. Lukic, you are fortunate that that has happened. The Chamber notes that the documents at issue here relate to alleged activities of the KLA in 1998 throughout Kosovo, and therefore they have a certain relevance and probative value; however, the Chamber must decide whether to exercise its discretion to add them to the list under the specific circumstances which apply. We've taken a lenient approach throughout the case to the amendment of 65 ter lists in order to avoid prejudice to the accused or procedural unfairness to the other parties. The Chamber also notes that the Prosecution has not taken a firm line to these types of motions by indicating on numerous occasions that it would not respond even when the documents have not been translated. However, the fact that documents were used in the Milosevic case does not remove the obligation of the Lukic Defence to provide adequate notice of the documents it intends to rely upon in presenting the evidence of any witness. The Chamber is of the view that the documents should have been disclosed far earlier in the case by the Lukic Defence -- should have been discovered far earlier in the case by the Lukic Defence in order to place the Prosecution as well as the other parties on adequate notice of them. This is even more important with the untranslated documents, which have not even been submitted for translation. The Chamber will, therefore, not allow amendment of the 65 ter list to include the 69 documents referred to. So far as the witness statement is concerned, although the guide-line we established, a 48-hour notice has not been complied with and no request has been made by the Lukic Defence for late intimation and thus admission of the statement. We will nevertheless allow that statement to be presented as part of the witness's evidence, but only to the extent that it relates to matters which are not affected by the need to amend the 65 ter list. We will thus order that the corresponding portions of the Rule 92 ter statement relating to these exhibits should be removed. We will then admit the remainder. So a revised copy of that statement will be required for tomorrow. The Chamber's determination, therefore, is that the motion to amend the exhibit list is denied, but without prejudice to any further application that might be made in relation to these documents or particular documents from among them. The Rule 92 ter statement in its current form is inadmissible, but once all references in the statements to the documents that have been denied, addition to the 65 ter list, and a new version has been submitted, the Chamber shall decide its admission status but anticipates admitting that redacted version. The parts which require to be removed are paragraph 13 from the words: "This is supported ..." to the end; paragraphs 14 to 15; paragraph 16 from the words, "Exhibit 6D1954" to the end; paragraph 17, 22 to 25, and 32. References to 6D614 which has featured frequently in the case may remain in the statement and the Chamber will issue a comprehensive order on this document in due course as we have previously indicated. That completes our sitting for today, and we shall resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 19th day of March, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.
